metadata.title: Monsters Among Us: Moral Nihilism, Misanthropy, and the Persistence of Racism
metadata.description:
This essay investigates the philosophical and psychological foundations that enable racism—and anti-Blackness in particular—to persist across generations despite legal, social, and educational advancements. Moving beyond conventional explanations rooted in ignorance, economic self-interest, or political manipulation, the author argues that racial hierarchy is sustained by a fundamental crisis of moral imagination, underpinned by two key dispositions: moral nihilism (the denial of inherent human worth) and misanthropy (a systemic distrust of human nature).

Drawing on Hannah Arendt’s concept of the "banality of evil" and Albert Bandura’s theory of "moral disengagement," the paper illustrates how ordinary individuals within institutional roles routinely perpetuate harm without experiencing themselves as cruel. It traces the historical adaptability of anti-Black systems—from chattel slavery and Jim Crow to modern algorithmic bias, environmental injustice, and housing discrimination—showing how the underlying commitment to Black exclusion continually reinvents itself. Finally, the essay explores internal responses to nihilistic conditions within Black intellectual and spiritual traditions, highlighting African humanism (Ubuntu), Black liberation theology, and bell hooks' ethic of love as vital frameworks for reclaiming non-contingent human dignity and resisting systemic dehumanization.

metadata.title: Beyond the Binary of Purity and Pollution: A Sociological Investigation of Contemporary  Neo-Dalit Movements and Digital Resistance in Urban India
metadata.description:
Abstract

This research investigates the profound paradigm shift in contemporary Dalit activism within urban India, moving beyond the traditional Dumontian frameworks of "purity and pollution" which have long dominated the sociological study of caste. Through a critical sociological lens, this paper examines how Neo-Dalit movements leverage digital platforms to construct powerful counter-narratives, mobilize collective identity, and systematically challenge structural inequalities within hyper-modern urban spaces. Utilizing a multi-sited, mixed-methods approach—combining digital ethnography, semi-structured qualitative interviews, and statistical content analysis—this study demonstrates that digital resistance is not merely a supplementary extension of physical protest but a fundamental, generative space for intersectional identity formation that transcends traditional, geographically bound caste hierarchies. Findings suggest that digital platforms facilitate a "virtuous cycle" of political mobilization, effectively connecting hyper-local grievances to expansive, national human rights discourses, thereby altering the traditional topography of power. The paper further critiques how algorithmic governance interacts with legacy social hierarchies, arguing that the digital realm acts simultaneously as an equalizer and a site of renewed structural contestation. By documenting the rise of "digital subalternity," this study provides a comprehensive roadmap for understanding the evolution of caste-based movements in the age of algorithmic capital, offering a new theoretical framework for interpreting the intersection of caste, technology, and urban citizenship.

Keywords: Neo-Dalit, Digital Resistance, Caste, Urban Sociology, Social Media Activism, India, Algorithmic Governance, Subalternity, Digital Public Sphere.

1. Introduction: The Evolving Landscape of Caste

The sociological discourse surrounding caste in India has historically been tethered to the binary of "purity and pollution," a conceptual framework popularized by Louis Dumont in Homo Hierarchicus. In this traditional view, the caste system was perceived as a rigid, ritualized, hierarchical order where social standing was inextricably linked to religious notions of sacred purity and profane impurity. This framework, while historically useful in mapping village-level social structures and the maintenance of traditional hegemony, often obscured the material basis of caste power, the endurance of untouchability in modern spheres, and the agency of those subjected to it.

In the 21st century, the rapid transformation of Indian urban centers—characterized by hyper-modernity, high-speed digital connectivity, and the emergence of a new "urban precariat"—requires a scholarly reappraisal of how caste operates. We are witnessing a transition from caste as a ritual hierarchy to caste as an algorithmic and structural barrier within the urban market economy. The digital age has introduced a new, complex topography of resistance that defies these rigid, traditional categories. Contemporary Neo-Dalit movements in urban India represent a radical departure from established, top-down caste-based organizational patterns, utilizing algorithmic visibility to bypass traditional media gatekeepers that have historically silenced or marginalized Dalit voices.

In the urban context, where anonymity and mobility often clash with lingering caste biases in housing, employment, and social life, the digital realm provides a persistent, accessible site for mobilization. The digital space is not merely a tool; it is an environment where the "politics of dignity" are re-articulated against the backdrop of an indifferent urban state. This paper argues that digital space serves as a "third space"—a hybrid, contested environment where traditional, stigmatized identities are actively deconstructed and new, assertive political subjectivities are forged. By examining the intricate interplay between virtual mobilization and urban structural inequality, we map how digital tools are reconfiguring the politics of dignity.

This investigation asks: How does the transition from physical spaces of exclusion to digital spaces of connection redefine the potential for democratic engagement among the marginalized? We explore how the digital realm allows for the creation of "counterpublics" where Ambedkarite ideologies are translated into viral messaging, effectively challenging the hegemony of traditional media and forcing state accountability in ways that were previously inaccessible to the subaltern. Furthermore, we contend that this shift is not purely emancipatory. As digital platforms become the primary arenas for sociopolitical discourse, they are subjected to algorithmic curation that often replicates, or even amplifies, the historical biases of the offline world. The "digital public sphere" in India is thus a site of intense friction, where the democratizing potential of global connectivity meets the persistence of localized, caste-based gatekeeping.

2. Methodology: Capturing the Digital Subaltern

This research adopts a rigorous triangulation of methods to capture the dynamism and volatility of digital activism across urban Indian centers. The approach acknowledges that digital data is not inherently objective but reflects the socio-technical biases of the platforms themselves.

Our methodology relies on the premise that the "digital subaltern" is a data-generating agent. Through deep-canvassing and digital ethnography, we traced the movement of hashtags like #DalitLivesMatter and #DalitHistoryMonth across diverse Indian urban hubs, accounting for regional variations in digital infrastructure and access. This methodological framework allows us to bridge the gap between abstract sociopolitical theory and the raw, granular data of contemporary digital life. By integrating these diverse methods, we gain a panoramic view of how digital activism functions both as a platform for discourse and as a tangible mechanism for legal and social change. We acknowledge the limitations of digital-only research, ensuring that our data is grounded in the lived realities of our participants, thereby validating digital findings through offline ethnographic cross-referencing.

3. Case Studies: The Digital Anatomy of Resistance

Case Study 1: The #DalitLivesMatter Campaign

This movement gained massive momentum in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bangalore, drawing critical parallels between global racial justice movements and Indian caste oppression. Unlike conventional protests, the campaign utilized "viral witnessing," where bystander videos of caste-based violence provided immediate, unfiltered evidence, forcing state accountability. The campaign forced mainstream media, often accused of ignoring caste atrocities, to engage with the reality of systematic violence, thus expanding the scope of the public conversation and creating a cross-generational dialogue about rights. By turning smartphones into tools of forensic accountability, the movement systematically dismantled the state’s monopoly on the "truth," compelling legal interventions where previously silence was the default. The campaign also served as a training ground for digital literacy, as activists developed sophisticated techniques to bypass content moderation filters that often disproportionately flag protest-related imagery.

Case Study 2: Digital Archiving Projects

Platforms such as "Dalit Camera" and various crowd-sourced archiving initiatives have pioneered the democratization of history. By capturing thousands of hours of oral histories from elderly community members, these projects create a non-institutional archive that challenges the sanitized, upper-caste historical narratives typically promoted by state hegemonies. This project of "counter-archiving" serves as a vital bulwark against historical erasure. It ensures that subaltern memory survives in the digital record, providing a repository for future generations to reclaim their heritage. This decentralization of the historical record is a profound rejection of the state's role as the sole arbiter of national memory. By transforming the "private" stories of discrimination into a "public" record, these archives force a re-evaluation of national milestones and symbols.

Case Study 3: Educational Advocacy Platforms

Digital mentorship networks serve as a critical, decentralized infrastructure for students entering higher education. By providing transparent, community-led resources on scholarships, entrance exam strategies, and networking, these platforms circumvent the informal, exclusive "caste-networks" (often referred to as 'merit' channels) that have historically barred Dalits from elite professional and academic spaces. This peer-to-peer knowledge sharing effectively levels the playing field, providing students with the "social capital" necessary to navigate institutional barriers that are often designed to exclude those without generational privilege. These networks demonstrate how digital community-building acts as a substitute for exclusionary kinship networks. As these networks scale, they have also begun to challenge the very definition of "merit," highlighting the structural barriers embedded in competitive exams.

Case Study 4: Urban Land Rights Activism

Using GIS-based digital mapping and community crowdsourcing, activists in peri-urban areas document state and private land encroachment. This "geo-resistance" allows communities to present localized, data-driven evidence in courts. By digitizing historical land deeds and overlaying them with real-time mapping technology, activists transform intangible, historical oral claims into actionable legal assets, effectively turning the digital map into a weapon of legal struggle. This application of technology bridges the gap between grassroots memory and formal legal requirements, transforming land struggles into technical, evidence-based disputes that are much harder for traditional power structures to dismiss. Through the synthesis of satellite imagery and community testimony, these projects expose the systematic displacement occurring under the guise of urban development.

5. Sociological Implications: Towards a New Theory of Agency

The findings suggest that digital resistance is not a peripheral activity but a central mechanism for contemporary Dalit assertion. By creating decentralized networks, activists are effectively "hacking" the social hierarchy. The digital space allows for a horizontal dissemination of information that bypasses the vertical power structures inherent in traditional caste society. However, this is tempered by the reality of digital surveillance and algorithmic bias, which continue to reflect the structural inequities of the physical world. The "digital divide" is not merely a lack of hardware; it is a manifestation of historical caste-based resource exclusion. As we transition into a digital-first governance model, the ability to command digital space becomes synonymous with the ability to participate in public life. Consequently, Neo-Dalit digital resistance serves as a corrective, an attempt to democratize a virtual landscape that threatens to replicate the exclusion of the physical one. This suggests a new theory of "networked agency" where the subaltern voice is not a singular cry but a distributed, persistent, and increasingly coordinated force that challenges the static, ritualized hierarchies of the past with a dynamic, fluid, and strategically mobilized present. The interplay of algorithmic capital and social identity suggests that the future of caste politics lies in the contestation of the digital architecture itself, requiring a deeper engagement with the politics of code, data ownership, and technological sovereignty.

Conclusion

Digital resistance represents a robust, multifaceted approach to challenging entrenched caste hegemony in urban India. By utilizing digital platforms, Neo-Dalit movements have successfully shifted the locus of political agency from traditional, rigid institutional structures to decentralized, networked spaces. This transformation has profound implications for urban democracy, suggesting that the "digital" is no longer a peripheral, passive space, but a core, active site where the future of caste, citizenship, and social justice is actively negotiated, contested, and ultimately redefined. The resilience shown by these movements suggests that even in a highly mediated world, the impulse toward equality remains the most potent, and now, the most viral, force in public life. The future of Dalit politics will increasingly rely on the navigation of these dual realities—the physical persistence of caste and the digital promise of liberation—ensuring that the struggle for annihilation of caste remains as current and vital as it has ever been. As technological integration deepens, the imperative for a nuanced, subaltern-informed digital policy becomes clear, framing the digital realm as a crucial, ongoing, and dynamic territory of liberation in the long, historic quest for dignity and equality.

metadata.title: biohttp: Normalized HTTP Transport with Circuit Breaking and Caching
metadata.description:
An HTTP transport layer for R clients of web services. Calls return a normalized result value rather than raising a condition, so transport failure, a non-success status code, and an unreadable response body are three distinct outcomes a caller can branch on.

Per-host circuit breaking, retry with a transient-failure predicate, optional throttling, redacted request headers, and a success-only cache come as defaults. Many questions to one source can be asked as a single batch, where only the entries the cache is missing reach the network. Service specific knowledge is left to the client packages built on top.

metadata.title: The Sociology of Collective Action in Women's Rights Movements
metadata.description:
Abstract 

This paper provides an exhaustive exploration of the theoretical frameworks and empirical dynamics of collective action within Indian women’s rights movements. By synthesizing Resource Mobilization Theory (RMT), Political Process Theory, and New Social Movement (NSM) theory, this study examines how Indian women’s groups navigate the complex, often contradictory intersections of caste, class, religious identity, and patriarchal structures to achieve legislative and social change. The paper traces the movement from the 19th-century social reform era to the post-colonial activism of the 1970s, and the contemporary digital-era protests. The findings suggest that Indian collective action is uniquely characterized by its integration into broader nationalist and local struggles, demonstrating that while institutional legal reform is a primary goal, the grassroots mobilization of marginalized women remains the movement's most resilient and transformative feature. This analysis further interrogates the "paradox of visibility" in the digital age, where global connectivity often clashes with the local, material realities of rural, Dalit, and Adivasi women, demanding a re-evaluation of what constitutes effective democratic participation in a deeply stratified society.

Keywords: Collective Action, Indian Feminism, Resource Mobilization, Political Opportunity Structure, Mathura Case, #MeToo India, Social Reform, Intersectionality, Caste-Gender Nexus.

1. Introduction: The Sociological Landscape of Indian Feminism

Collective action in the Indian context is inextricably linked to the history of anti-colonial resistance and the subsequent quest for democratic equity in a post-colonial state. Unlike Western social movements, which have often been analyzed through the lens of individual rights and civil liberties, Indian women’s movements frequently operate through the lens of community, social reform, and state-led development. The Indian trajectory is one of "negotiated modernity," where activists navigate a state that is simultaneously a vehicle for emancipation and a site of patriarchal control.

This paper investigates the sociological mechanisms that transform latent grievances into active mobilization across three distinct, yet overlapping, phases: the pre-independence reform movement, the post-colonial struggle, and the contemporary era of globalized digital activism. By examining these phases, we gain insight into how movements adapt to changing political opportunity structures, technological shifts, and the persistent challenge of intersectionality where gendered oppression is inextricably mediated by caste hierarchy and economic deprivation. Unlike more monolithic Western movements, the Indian experience is defined by its deep fragmentation along lines of caste, religious communalism, and economic inequality, necessitating a more complex sociological assessment of what constitutes "collective" action.

We must examine how the "woman question" was historically constructed and how contemporary movements are dismantling these colonial-era binaries to create a more inclusive, ground-up democratic discourse. Furthermore, the role of the Indian state as an arbiter of gender justice often through the enactment of protective legislation creates a unique dynamic where the movement must constantly challenge the state while also lobbying it for enforcement and expansion. The sociology of these movements is not merely a record of protests but an inquiry into the very definition of citizenship in a diverse, post-colonial society. The fundamental sociological question here is: how does a movement achieve cohesion when the very identity of "woman" is contested by competing visions of caste, religion, and regional autonomy?

2. Theoretical Frameworks in the Indian Context

2.1 Theoretical Adaptation and the "Fluidity" of Indian Movements

The application of Western social movement theory to India requires significant adaptation. Movements in India often exist in a state of "fluidity," where the distinction between formal organizations and informal networks is blurred. Often, the "movement" is not a formal NGO but a loosely organized collective of women responding to a local crisis, making traditional organizational analysis less predictive.

Table 1: Theoretical Adaptation and the "Fluidity" of Indian Movements

Theory

Indian Contextual Application

Analytical Focus

Resource Mobilization (RMT)

Reliance on voluntary labor, self-help groups, and local networks.

Examining how groups sustain themselves despite limited state or private funding.

Political Process

Movements capitalize on "state-feminism" and the Indian judiciary.

Evaluating how activists leverage judicial activism and PILs to bypass legislative inertia.

New Social Movement (NSM)

Focus on identity (caste/religion/region) as much as gender.

Analyzing how "the personal is political" takes on a cultural, non-material dimension.

2.2 The Intersectionality Lens and the Caste-Gender Nexus

Crucially, this analysis adopts an intersectional framework, drawing from Dalit feminist theory (e.g., Gopal Guru, Sharmila Rege). This recognizes that a "universal" Indian woman does not exist; instead, the collective action of Brahminical, upper-caste urban women often diverges from the grassroots, survival-based resistance of Dalit and Adivasi women. The "Caste-Gender Nexus" is a unique dimension where the control of female sexuality is essential to the maintenance of caste purity, making Indian feminist collective action inherently an anti-caste project. In India, gender is not a standalone identity; it is filtered through the rigid hierarchies of the caste system, where upper-caste women are often the custodians of ritual purity, while Dalit women face a "triple burden" of caste-based violence, economic exploitation, and patriarchal subjugation. This theoretical shift allows us to move beyond the monolithic "woman" and recognize the divergent, yet interconnected, paths of resistance.

The implications for collective action are significant: mobilization cannot succeed if it ignores the structural reality of the caste system. If feminism in India is to be democratic, it must acknowledge that the patriarchal violence faced by an upper-caste woman in a corporate office is qualitatively different from the systemic, state-sanctioned violence faced by a Dalit woman in a rural village. Therefore, the "collective" in Indian women’s movements is a fragile, heterogeneous entity that requires constant negotiation of power and privilege.

3. Historical Phases of Collective Action

3.1 Phase I: Social Reform and Nationalism (19th Century – 1947)

Collective action in this era was largely "top-down," led by male reformers such as Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who sought to "uplift" women to modernize the Indian domestic sphere in line with colonial expectations. However, by the early 20th century, women began asserting their own agency. Organizations like the All India Women’s Conference (AIWC) were established, initially focusing on education and suffrage. The "woman question" was central to nationalist discourse, framed as a litmus test for the civilization of the Indian people. Women joined the Gandhian struggle in unprecedented numbers, blending domestic struggle with the fight for Swaraj. This era demonstrated that women's mobilization could be simultaneously conservative (in terms of family roles) and radical (in terms of political anti-colonialism). This period established the template of "protective legislation" as a primary goal, which continues to shape the movement's relationship with the state today.

3.2 Phase II: The 1970s and the "Autonomous" Women's Movement

The post-1975 period, the era of the Emergency, saw a radical explosion of autonomous women's groups. This phase moved away from the moderate reformism of the past. The landmark Towards Equality report (1974) provided the empirical data necessary to challenge state failure. The movement during this period was characterized by "consciousness-raising," a direct import of global feminist practices, but localized through campaigns against dowry deaths, custodial rape, and communal violence. Groups like Saheli and Stree Sangharsh pioneered new modes of protesting, moving from street-corner plays to legal advocacy, cementing the role of the feminist collective as an alternative social support system. This era fundamentally shifted the focus from asking the state for "protection" to challenging the state's role in perpetrating violence.

3.3 Phase III: Contemporary Digital and Globalized Activism

The 2012 Delhi gang rape case and the subsequent #MeToo India movement represents a transition to "Connective Action." This phase relies on social media to bypass traditional media gatekeepers. However, this transition is double-edged; while digital platforms offer unprecedented reach, they risk "slacktivism" and often prioritize the narratives of urban, English-speaking elites, potentially overshadowing the material realities of rural women. This era necessitates a sociological examination of how "digital intimacy" replaces physical, grounded solidarity, and whether it can effectively challenge the deep-seated structural patriarchy of the Indian hinterlands. The digital sphere acts as a megaphone for some, but a barrier for those without the cultural and linguistic capital to navigate it.

4. Case Studies of Mobilization

4.1 The Mathura Rape Case (1979-1980)

The Mathura Rape Case (1979-1980) serves as a foundational juncture for Indian legal feminism, emerging from the acquittal of two policemen accused of the custodial rape of a young Dalit girl. This judicial verdict triggered widespread nationwide indignation, as it crystallized the systemic failure of the state to protect women from custodial violence, specifically by highlighting the inherent power asymmetry within the state-citizen relationship. The movement represents a quintessential application of the "Political Opportunity Structure" theory, as activists transformed a single, egregious instance of judicial miscarriage into a sustained, national campaign for legislative transformation. By navigating the corridors of legalism, the movement successfully shifted the burden of proof and challenged the colonial-era definitions of consent that had previously obfuscated the reality of custodial power. The subsequent agitation forced the Indian legislature to confront the limitations of existing penal codes, ultimately culminating in the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act of 1983. This legislative victory was not merely a result of reactive public anger; rather, it was the product of a sophisticated, organized effort that utilized consciousness-raising and public documentation to hold the state accountable for its complicity in violence. The Mathura case established a model for future collective action, demonstrating how civil society can effectively manipulate political openings to compel structural amendments to the Indian Penal Code. It highlighted that institutional reform in India often requires the mobilization of both legal expertise and grassroots indignation. Consequently, the case transcended its original grievance, forcing the legal system to formalize a new discourse regarding state accountability, custodial rights, and the bodily autonomy of women. It remains a seminal example of how a singular, traumatic event can be transmuted into a long-term, systemic reform process, signaling the rise of a more assertive, rights-based feminist movement that was no longer willing to operate within the passive confines of traditional institutional benevolence. The case stands as a testament to the fact that when institutional silence is confronted with organized, sustained defiance, the state can be compelled to rewrite the legal terms of its relationship with its marginalized citizens.

4.2 The Anti-Arrack Movement (1990s)

The Anti-Arrack movement in Andhra Pradesh during the 1990s stands as a definitive sociological testament to the transformative power of grassroots, community-led resistance against systemic patriarchal and economic oppression. Emerging from rural villages, this movement was not merely a reaction to alcohol consumption but a sophisticated socio-economic critique that linked the proliferation of arrack (locally distilled alcohol) directly to cycles of domestic violence, household impoverishment, and the systematic erosion of female domestic authority. Rural women, often marginalized within formal political discourses, recognized that the state’s reliance on excise revenue from alcohol sales commodified their suffering for fiscal gain. By mobilizing through local networks and leveraging the collective strength of their numbers, these women initiated a form of "everyday resistance" that transcended passive protest. They systematically disrupted the supply chains of local liquor vendors and held public demonstrations that forced the state to confront its own complicity in the domestic suffering of its citizens. This mobilization was not guided by abstract ideological slogans or elite political agendas; rather, it was deeply rooted in the immediate, material realities of survival and the urgent need for domestic safety. The success of the movement in compelling the state government to implement a blanket ban on arrack sales remains a seminal example of how subaltern groups can effectively penetrate and alter the political opportunity structure. It highlights the crucial necessity of local autonomy, proving that the most resilient feminist movements in India often derive their transformative energy from the localized labor of marginalized communities who directly confront the nexus of state policy and structural patriarchy. Through this sustained, on-the-ground labor, the movement achieved what formal institutional channels often fail to realize: a tangible, state-level policy shift driven by the unified, assertive agency of the very women it sought to regulate.

5. Discussion: The Paradox of Visibility

The contemporary Indian women's movement is currently confronted by the distinct, often stifling "paradox of visibility" inherent to the digital age. While social media and digital platforms have drastically accelerated the velocity and reach of mobilization, this rapid-fire engagement does not inherently translate into tangible, structural policy reform. A persistent "class-caste divide" remains deeply embedded within the digital sphere, creating a hierarchy of participation where the voices of urban, English-speaking elites frequently drown out the material realities of rural, Dalit, and Adivasi women. True collective action in the Indian context cannot rely solely on the ephemeral nature of viral hashtags or performative digital solidarity. Rather, it must sustain its transformative energy by effectively bridging the chasm between digital "viral" visibility and the entrenched, long-term, on-the-ground labor that defines grassroots feminist organizations. We are compelled to critically interrogate whose voices are being amplified by algorithmic gatekeepers, and conversely, whose experiences remain persistently silenced in the era of algorithmic activism. The current digital landscape mandates a deeply reflexive approach—one that actively acknowledges the severe digital divide, recognizing that technological access is not distributed equitably across socio-economic strata. We must ensure that the most marginalized voices are not merely treated as passive data points or "trending topics" for consumption by a digital audience. Instead, these communities must be centered as active, contributing agents of structural change. For the movement to thrive, technology must function as a multiplier for traditional, localized organizing, rather than a convenient replacement for the essential, localized labor of feminist resistance. Ultimately, the challenge lies in converting digital fleeting attention into an enduring, substantive influence upon the state’s developmental and legislative agenda.

Conclusion

The sociology of Indian women's movements is a study of persistence amidst immense structural complexity. Successful collective action in India requires a synthesis of grassroots cultural identity, persistent engagement with the judiciary, and the strategic use of modern digital infrastructure. Future movements must ensure that digital reach does not sideline the material, intersectional concerns of marginalized women. The path forward lies in integrating the digital with the local, ensuring that the technology of connection serves the foundational needs of justice and equity for all women, regardless of caste or geography. By reconciling the historical legacy of social reform with the contemporary urgency of intersectional justice, Indian feminist movements continue to reshape the very definition of democracy.

This article analyzes the impact of disinformation and fake news circulating on social networks on public moral security. metadata.title: Phenotypic plasticity and cryptic generic enigma in Pleosporales: Establishing Sporidesmioidesaceae fam. nov. and Rostriconidium synnematicum sp. nov. from India
metadata.description: This study reappraised the taxonomy of the genus Rostriconidium, and introduced a new species, Rostriconidium synnematicum, based on an integrated molecular and morphological taxonomic approach. This new taxon is the only synnematous species within Rostriconidium and forms a sister lineage to other Rostriconidium species in Torulaceae, as supported by phylogenetic analyses of ITS, LSU, SSU, rpb2 and tef1-α sequences using Maximum Likelihood and Bayesian Inference methods. Additionally, a new combination Rostriconidium yunnanensis is proposed under Rostriconidium. The study addresses the taxonomic complexities of four morphologically similar but phylogenetically distinct genera (Neopodoconis, Pseudohelminthosporium, Rostriconidium, and Sporidesmioides) within the Pleosporales. There are a few taxonomic challenges in resolving relationships among these genera, given their polyphyletic nature and overlapping morphologies. In this study, advanced mycological studies were conducted to resolve the generic circumscription of Sporidesmioides. In this study, we propose a new familial lineage, Sporidesmioidesaceae, to accommodate the monotypic species S. thailandica, based on phylogenetic analyses of a multi-locus dataset (ITS, LSU, SSU, rpb2, and tef1-α). The results also accommodate Pseudohelminthosporium within Neomassarinaceae, rather than accepting the synonymization of Pseudohelminthosporium clematidis under Neopodoconis ampullacea. The conspecific nature of P. clematidis and N. ampullacea warrants a future type-based study to validate them. These findings underscore the critical importance of examining type specimens (morphological and multi-locus sequence analysis) before proposing synonymy among cryptic species and genera. This study also revalidated the placement of the recently proposed family Megacapitulaceae and provided their multigene sequence information.

metadata.title: Two novel species of Sympoventuriaceae from palms in China
metadata.description:
Palm plants (Arecaceae) are widely distributed ornamental hosts in southern China. However, most of these plants are introduced species, and their associated microfungal diversity remains poorly understood. In this study, four strains with morphological affinities to Scolecobasidium and Yunnanomyces (Sympoventuriaceae) were isolated from palm plants in Yunnan Province, China. Two novel species, Scolecobasidium yunnanense and Yunnanomyces didymosporus, are proposed based on morphological observations and separate multi-locus phylogenetic analyses: the phylogeny of Scolecobasidium was constructed from a concatenated ITS + nLSU + tub2 + tef1-α dataset, while analyses for Yunnanomyces within Sympoventuriaceae relied on a combined ITS + nLSU + nrSSU + RPB2 dataset. Scolecobasidium yunnanense is characterized by its branched, septate, thick-walled pale hyphae, erect, unbranched and septate conidiophores often reduced to denticulate conidiogenous cells, and smooth, mostly 2-septate, ellipsoidal to fusiform conidia, measuring 8.3–12.6 × 2.0–3.5 μm. Yunnanomyces didymosporus is characterized by its monilioid mature hyphae, intercalary conidiogenous cells, and chain-forming mostly 1-septate conidia with a dark hilum on one or both ends, measuring 6.1–11.9 × 2.0–4.2 μm.

The study confirms their distinctiveness from extant species within each genus and enhances the understanding of microfungal diversity associated with palms.

metadata.title: Astragalus baimaensis (Fabaceae), a new species from Yunnan, China
metadata.description: Based on an integrative analysis of morphological traits and molecular phylogenetic evidence, a new species of Astragalus (Fabaceae), A. baimaensis B. Jiang & Y. Z. Zhang, discovered during field investigations in the Baima Mountain region, Deqin County, Yunnan Province, China, is formally described. This species is defined by a unique combination of diagnostic morphological characters that unequivocally distinguish it from all previously documented congeners: it is completely glabrous throughout, with narrowly oblong leaflets, yellow flowers, and obliquely ellipsoid, glabrous, inflated legumes. The full chloroplast genome of A. baimaensis is 124,633 bp in length. Phylogenetic reconstructions based on plastid genomic data resolve A. baimaensis as sister to A. tongolensis, whereas analyses of the combined nuclear ITS and plastid (rbcL, matK) multilocus dataset support a closer evolutionary affinity between A. baimaensis and A. chilienshanensis. Despite these close phylogenetic relationships, the new species exhibits a distinct set of consistent morphological differences that clearly distinguish it from both putative relatives. The results highlight the considerable taxonomic value of variation in ovary pubescence within Astragalus and confirm that the presence or absence of trichomes on the ovary represents a stable diagnostic trait for species delimitation and infrageneric classification in this genus. This study adds to the known diversity of Astragalus and provides data for future phylogenetic and ecological studies.
